contentBlocks.text: Last week you mastered the data-science inquiry cycle. This week: statistical inference, the course's other core thread!

A population is the entire group you want to learn about, while a sample is a smaller subset actually measured — since measuring an entire population is often impossible or impractical, statisticians use a well-chosen sample to make inferences (educated conclusions) about the whole population, connecting directly to last week's sampling-bias content. A school wants to know the average time students spend on homework. Explain why surveying every single student (the population) might be impractical, and what a good sample would need to look like instead.
You just reviewed population vs. sample! Tomorrow we'll learn why sample-based estimates carry real uncertainty.

objectives: Distinguish a population from a sample
Explain why surveying an entire population is often impractical and what a good sample requires
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review last week's sampling-bias content briefly.
2. Introduce population vs. sample using the homework-time example.
3. Have the child explain why full-population surveying is often impractical.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's uncertainty lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use a simple concrete number — if a school has 2,000 students, ask how long it would realistically take to survey every single one
Ready for more: ask the child what could go wrong if the sample only included students from one grade level, rather than a genuine cross-section
Opens this week's statistical-inference thread from the course's own description, directly building on last week's sampling content
teacherGuide.answerKey: Surveying every single student would take enormous time and effort, especially in a large school — a good sample instead needs to be representative, including a genuine cross-section of students across grades, backgrounds, and habits, so the sample's results reasonably reflect the whole population rather than just one narrow group.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Statistics standard S-IC.1: understanding statistics as a process for making inferences about population parameters based on a random sample, opening this week's thread from the course's own description.
